summary: Angel and Jeff visit Tim and Kirsten at their new secret apartment in the Tenderloin district. The chapter captures the strange domesticity of the affair and Tim's continued intellectual preoccupations. Tim is discovered to be taking Dexamyl (amphetamines), having traded his former alcoholism for speed addiction. The chapter includes Tim's discussion of the Zadokite Documentsâ€”ancient scrolls containing the word 'anokhi' (Hebrew for 'I,' the Divine Name) used in unprecedented ways by the ancient Zadokite sect. These documents suggest a pre-Christian knowledge of the Divine Self-consciousness, potentially predating and superseding Christian orthodoxy. Tim's enthusiasm for music (Janis Joplin, Frank Zappa, T. Rex) reveals his perpetual naivetÃ© and his dependence on Kirsten and Angel to guide him through contemporary culture. The chapter establishes Tim's alienation from material realityâ€”he cannot manage details, losing track of basic information. Jeff appears increasingly moody and withdrawn, sensing his exclusion from his father's theological and emotional life.

narrative_observations: This chapter establishes the theological and historical MacGuffin that will drive the plot: the Zadokite Documents and their central usage of 'anokhi.' The chapter also demonstrates Tim's character more fullyâ€”his brilliance coupled with complete emotional and practical incompetence. His need for Kirsten and Angel to manage the world around him explains his attraction to Kirsten. The chapter introduces the temporal structure of the novel: events in London (where Tim and Kirsten will travel) will remain largely unknown to the reader, creating a mystery about what Tim discovered and how it transformed his understanding. Jeff's emotional state is carefully trackedâ€”his withdrawal foreshadows his later suicide.
